title: One vehicle (Kern ch. 2)
hook: the three vehicles were skillful means; really there is one vehicle to Buddhahood for all

segments.voice: Yesterday, upaya: the Buddhas teach in many shapes, fitted to whoever is listening. Your line: many ways, one goal. Did you try a new way of saying something? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

Three travelers board a train through three different doors: one at the front, one in the middle, one at the back. Each settles in and thinks of it as their own car. Then the conductor walks through and says: it's one train, going to one station. The doors were only so you could all get on. That is roughly the moment chapter two of the Lotus Sutra builds to. Yesterday the Buddha said he teaches in many ways. Today he says what the ways were for, and it unsettles some of the people who had been walking longest. Today: one vehicle.
screen: `THREE DOORS, THREE CARS.` → `IT WAS ONE TRAIN.` → `WHAT THE DOORS WERE FOR.`

segments.voice: First, the three vehicles. Buddhist teaching speaks of different paths, called vehicles, yana in Sanskrit, the word for a cart or a carriage. The Lotus names three: the vehicle of the disciples who hear the teaching, the vehicle of those who awaken on their own, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. Different travelers, different carts. Second, the reveal. In chapter two the Buddha tells Sariputra plainly: there is only one vehicle, the Buddha-vehicle. Not a second, not a third. The three were skillful means, upaya, offered because people differ in what they can hear. Underneath them, the destination is the same for everyone: Buddhahood itself. That is ekayana, the one vehicle. Third, who gets in. The sutra keeps widening the door, almost playfully. In Kern's translation the Buddha describes people who once made a small offering at a shrine, or bowed, or raised a hand, or said a single word of honor to the Buddha, even children who piled up sand as a stupa while they played. All of them, the sutra says, have reached awakening. The vehicle has room for the child in the sandbox. Fourth, the sharp edge. In the sutra's own story, this is not a soft message. It tells disciples who had worked hard toward their own goal that the goal was a stopping place, not the end. Buddhist schools read this differently. Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren teachers put the one vehicle at the center of their teaching. The Lotus is not part of the Theravada canon, and Theravada teachers describe the path in their own terms. Today simply hears what the Lotus says, in its own voice. Tomorrow's chapter turns all of this into a story, so it can be carried home: a house, a fire, some children, and carts.
screen: `THREE VEHICLES, THREE CARTS.` · `REALLY THERE IS ONE.` · `EVEN A CHILD'S SAND STUPA.` · `SCHOOLS READ IT THEIR OWN WAY.` · then, large: `ONE VEHICLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: see one path under many. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind a few people you know who look for meaning in very different ways: one who prays, one who runs, one who paints, one who simply cares for others. Let each picture come and rest a moment. Then, without deciding anything about them, ask quietly: what might they be walking toward? Notice whether any answer comes. If none does, just rest in the question. The bell holds the time.
Ekayana. The one vehicle: in the Lotus Sutra, the teaching that the many paths were skillful means, and all of them carry to the same awakening. Today's word.
Your line: one vehicle. Today, when you notice two people going about something in opposite ways, look for the one thing they both want. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: In the Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren schools the one vehicle of the Lotus Sutra is a central teaching, studied as the meaning beneath all the Buddha's other teachings; Theravada Buddhists do not use the Lotus Sutra as scripture.

fork.setup: you have spent years on the disciples' path toward your own release. the Buddha says there is only one vehicle. what does that mean for your goal?
options: it was the wrong path all along
it was a resting place, and the road goes on to Buddhahood
fork.reveal: in the Lotus the earlier paths were skillful means, not mistakes; the one vehicle carries everyone further, to Buddhahood itself.

original.note: Sanskrit: eka, one, plus yana, vehicle; the Lotus Sutra's one Buddha-vehicle.

trapdoor: what you thought: one vehicle means everyone must practice the same way.
what it means: in the Lotus, the Buddha's own different teachings were skillful means, and they all lead to one goal, Buddhahood.
what a scholar hears: ekayana reframes the three Buddhist vehicles as upaya; the ways stay many while the goal is one, and schools such as Tiantai built their teaching around it.
